input.question: Oracle v. Google Law Suit
input.ground_truth: Oracle bought a company called Sun. Sun had developed a programming language called Java. Google had introduced an operating system for mobile phones called Andorid. Android is built on top of a variant of Java. Android started to become very valuable and Oracle wanted to get some of that money. Oracle claimed that Android used some things from Java that Oracle didn't explicitly license them to use. Google disagreed. A court decided, largely in favor of Google.

Question: Oracle v. Google Law Suit

Answer:

response.prediction: In the Oracle v. Google lawsuit, Oracle accused Google of copyright infringement because Google used some of the code and structure from Oracle’s Java software in creating Android. Google argued that this was allowed under the “fair use” doctrine, especially since they only used certain parts and it was necessary for making Android work with existing Java programs. The courts were divided, but eventually the U.S. Supreme Court decided not to hear the case, allowing a lower court’s ruling to stand. That ruling said Google did not infringe on copyright because the parts they used were not protected and because their use was fair. So, in the end, Google was allowed to use those parts of Java in Android.
